record.label: Plateau-preserving approximation and curvature identity
record.statement: For gamma in U equal to c>0 on an open interval I contained in (0,1), every t in I has a closed neighborhood on which positive bounded nondecreasing finite-step approximants remain exactly c, with terminal smoothing M_n>=||gamma_n||infinity and M_n->infinity. Spatial derivatives and bounded polynomial moments along coupled paths converge there. With r=cPhi_x, v=r_x, w=r_xx, z=r_xxx, Phi_xx>0 and c^2 q'''(t)=E[z^2-12v*w^2+6v^4].
record.boundary: Curated source-level mathematical statement, not an elaborated Lean extraction or independently accepted proof. Its displayed local hypotheses are quantified guards; a hypothetical plateau is not an added premise of the full-support theorem. The interval hypothesis supplies continuity at t; this is important for the corresponding Lean coercivity source. Only derivative moments through order four pass to the limit, with one further derivative bound for path evaluation; no density-score convergence is asserted. The c=0 case is separate.

aligned_passages.text:
The curvature argument needs estimates uniform over the approximating
coefficients. Here is the route from the control formula to those estimates;
all bounds are taken on a fixed strip ending before time one.

For finite-step coefficients and a smooth, even, convex, one-Lipschitz
terminal function $\psi$, the evolution through a step of height $c$ is
$$
\Phi(t,x)=
\begin{cases}
c^{-1}\log P_{b-t}(e^{c\Phi(b,\cdot)})(x),&c>0,\\
P_{b-t}\Phi(b,\cdot)(x),&c=0,
\end{cases}
$$
where $P_h$ denotes convolution with a centred Gaussian of variance $h$.
The heat formula preserves evenness, convexity and the spatial Lipschitz
bound. Along a controlled path $dY_s=\gamma(s)\alpha_s\,ds+dB_s$, the drift
of the value minus the accumulated control cost is
$-\gamma(s)(\alpha_s-\Phi_x(s,Y_s))^2/2$. It is nonpositive, and is zero
for the feedback control. This proves the stated control formula for the
smooth step problem, including attainability by its feedback diffusion.

Using the same control in two such problems and then taking suprema gives
$$
\|\Phi_{\gamma,\psi}-\Phi_{\widetilde\gamma,\widetilde\psi}\|_\infty
\le \|\psi-\widetilde\psi\|_\infty
       +\frac32\|\gamma-\widetilde\gamma\|_{L^1(0,1)}.
$$
The drift part costs at most the coefficient difference in $L^1$, by the
terminal Lipschitz bound; the quadratic cost contributes another half of
that difference. The supremum norm is of the difference of the values,
which is bounded even though each value grows linearly in $x$.
With $\psi_M(x)=M^{-1}\log(2\cosh Mx)$,
$0\le\psi_M-|x|\le(\log2)/M$. Choose simultaneously $\gamma_m\to\gamma$ in $L^1$ and $M_m\to\infty$.
These are two distinct requirements: $M_m\ge\|\gamma_m\|_\infty$ alone
does not force terminal convergence. This compatible approximation
determines a unique uniform limiting value. Its terminal bound,
given in §2.2, also follows directly: choose the zero control for the lower
bound, and use $|\alpha|-\alpha^2/2\le1/2$ for the upper bound.

To obtain spatial derivatives, choose $T<b<1$. Monotonicity gives the
uniform coefficient estimate
$$
\gamma(t)\le\frac{\|\gamma\|_1}{1-b}\quad(0\le t\le b).
$$
An $L^1$-convergent family thus has a common coefficient bound $\Gamma$ on
this larger strip. For its smooth step approximants, put $U=\Phi_x$.
The differentiated mild equation is
$$
U(t)=P_{b-t}U(b)+\int_t^b\gamma(s)P_{s-t}[U(s)U_x(s)]\,ds.
$$
Since $\|U\|_\infty\le1$ and
$\|\partial_xP_hF\|_\infty\le Ch^{-1/2}\|F\|_\infty$,
$$
\|U_x(t)\|_\infty\le\frac C{\sqrt{b-t}}
 +C\Gamma\int_t^b\frac{\|U_x(s)\|_\infty}{\sqrt{s-t}}\,ds.
$$
Substituting this inequality once into its own integral uses
$\int_t^s((r-t)(s-r))^{-1/2}\,dr=\pi$. It reduces the estimate to an
ordinary backward Gronwall inequality with integrable forcing. This bounds
$U_x$ uniformly on $[0,T]$ without any terminal derivative bound. Repeating
on successively smaller strips bounds each higher spatial derivative: put
one derivative on the heat kernel and the rest on $UU_x$; only the term
$U\partial_x^mU$ contains the new highest derivative. The remaining products
have already been bounded.

Uniform convergence of the values then yields convergence of every
positive spatial derivative. For a bounded twice differentiable difference
$F$ with bounded second derivative, Taylor's formula gives
$$
\|F'\|_\infty\le \frac{2\|F\|_\infty}{h}
                         +\frac h2\|F''\|_\infty\qquad(h>0).
$$
First choose $h$ small using the common second-derivative bound, then make
$\|F\|_\infty$ small. Iterate on derivative differences. Passing to the
integral form of the differentiated PDE proves local absolute continuity
in time and its almost-everywhere equations. No classical time derivative
at a coefficient jump, and no derivative of $|x|$ at its cusp, is being
assumed.

Finally, couple all feedback diffusions with the same Brownian motion.
On $[0,T]$, let $L$ be a common spatial Lipschitz bound for their drifts.
The difference of the two integral equations gives, for example,
$$
\sup_{s\le T}|X_s^n-X_s|
\le e^{LT}\left(\|\gamma_n-\gamma\|_1
 +\|\gamma_n\|_1\|u_n-u\|_{\infty,[0,T]\times\mathbb R}\right)
 \longrightarrow0.
$$
This is a deterministic bound under the coupling. The derivative bounds
one order higher ensure uniform continuity when derivatives are evaluated
at these moving points. Every fixed polynomial in the bounded derivatives
therefore converges in expectation. This is precisely the convergence
needed for the integrated curvature expression in §4; none of the forward
density scores or their quotients need converge.
[OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.3][fs-reg].

### 2.5 Order of approximation

The same symbol for a small error must not conceal changing background
objects. The following account fixes those objects before the indicated
limit. A single admissible minimiser and its associated diffusion are
retained throughout the scalar construction.

**Compact-strip regularity.** Fix a derivative order $k\ge1$, a cutoff
$T<1$ and a common coefficient $L^1$ bound. Coefficients converge in $L^1$
within that bound; spatial derivatives converge uniformly on the strip.

**Shape inequalities on a plateau.** Fix the height $c>0$ and a closed
interior neighbourhood. Choose step coefficients equal to $c$ there and
smooth terminal values with $M_m\ge\|\gamma_m\|_\infty$ and
$M_m\to\infty$. The coefficient and terminal approximations may be
chosen as one compatible sequence.

**First variation.** Fix $\gamma$, a feasible $\eta\in L^1$ and initially
$\epsilon>0$. Remove the terminal cutoff before letting
$\epsilon\downarrow0$. The terminal remainder divided by $\epsilon$ is
bounded by an $L^1$ tail of $\eta$.

**Terminal value.** Keep the chosen minimiser and diffusion fixed. Bounded
martingale convergence and integrability of $\gamma$ justify
$t\uparrow1$; no terminal derivative bound is needed.

**Finite Gaussian coefficients.** Fix $\gamma,X$ and $T<1$. Refine $N$
using the fixed-strip bounds, then control the remaining value tail by $1-T$.

For the plateau transfer, tail estimates for a fixed approximant may depend
on that approximant. The passage to the limit uses the integrated
polynomial in the scaled second, third and fourth spatial derivatives of
the value function and the common strip bounds; it does not require
uniform bounds on the auxiliary density scores. Sections 3 and 4 explain
the variation and plateau-transfer arguments, and §7 gives a complete scalar error
budget. The further choices used to produce a circuit appear in §8.6.
[OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.1, Lemma 6.1, Proposition 5.1 and
Proposition 7.2][fs-main].

The quantity used in both arguments is a spatial moment. Recall $a=\Phi_{xx}$, write $b=\Phi_{xxx}$ and $d=\Phi_{xxxx}$, and, for $00$. For its associated diffusion, $$ \mathcal C_\gamma(t)\geq\frac{c^2}{1000} \mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]. $$ Neither minimality nor a constant neighbourhood of $t$ is required. This is the consequence of [OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 5.1 and Lemmas 2.1–2.2][FS] stated in the companion's [Proposition 4.1, §4.5](../long/reasoning-record.md#fixed-time-coercivity). We first explain the positive-plateau estimate, then obtain this fixed-time form by inserting a short plateau. For a smooth coefficient the identity connecting the two applications is $$ q'''+2\gamma'\mathbb E a^3=\mathcal C_\gamma. $$ On a plateau, $\gamma'=0$; at a smooth minimiser, full support gives $q=t$ and hence $q'''=0$. Section 4 proves the required smoothness before using the second identity. On a plateau with $\gamma=c>0$, put $r=c\Phi_x=c u$, $v=r_x=c a$, $w=r_{xx}$ and $z=r_{xxx}$. This rescaling makes the derivative identities polynomial. The PDE becomes $r_t=-\tfrac12r_{xx}-rr_x$, and the diffusion has spatial generator $\tfrac12\partial_{xx}+r\partial_x$. Differentiating in space and applying Itô's formula gives the drift and diffusion pairs $(0,v)$, $(-v^2,w)$ and $(-3vw,z)$ for $r,v,w$, respectively. All expectations in this section evaluate spatial functions at $(t,X_t)$. Starting with $c^2q'=\mathbb E v^2$, Itô's formula gives $$ \begin{aligned} c^2q''&=\mathbb E[w^2-2v^3],\\ c^2q'''&=\mathbb E[z^2-12vw^2+6v^4] =c^2\mathcal C_\gamma(t). \end{aligned} \tag{4} $$ For example, the drifts of $w^2$ and $v^3$ are $z^2-6vw^2$ and $3vw^2-3v^4$, respectively. The negative mixed term is the obstacle. Convexity, which gives $v\geq0$, does not control it. Indeed, for the smooth auxiliary terminal value $\log(2\cosh x)$ and coefficient $\gamma\equiv1$, the solution is $\Phi(t,x)=\log(2\cosh x)+(1-t)/2$. Thus $r=\tanh x$; at $r^2=1/2$, the polynomial in (4) equals $-19/8$. This is a finite-step smoothing example, not a minimiser of the absolute-value-terminal problem; its calculation is given in [long §4.1](../long/reasoning-record.md#curvature-moments). The same section gives a negative pointwise value with the actual $|x|$ terminal datum for a small positive constant coefficient ([long §4.1, pointwise obstruction](../long/reasoning-record.md#pointwise-curvature-obstruction)). The proof subtracts a weighted divergence whose expectation under the law of $X_t$ is zero. The resulting expression has a positive fourth-moment remainder. The backward value function and the forward density must satisfy joint shape restrictions for this decomposition to have the required signs. Those comparisons and the exact polynomial identity are the substantial inputs from [OpenAI (2026a), §§3–4][FS]. We explain their roles first for finite-step coefficients, then pass the integrated inequality to an integrable coefficient by approximation. Begin with a positive nondecreasing finite-step coefficient $\gamma_{\rm step}$: a function constant on each interval of a finite partition. Replace the terminal value $|x|$ by the smooth approximation $M^{-1}\log(2\cosh Mx)$, with $M\geq\|\gamma_{\rm step}\|_\infty$. On a step of height $c$, set $h=e^{c\Phi}$. Then $h_t=-h_{xx}/2$ and $r=h_x/h$. The same exponential removes the drift from the forward density equation. Indeed, writing $f=hg$ gives $$ \begin{aligned} f_t&=\tfrac12(hg)_{xx}-(h_xg)_x\\ &=-\tfrac12h_{xx}g+\tfrac12hg_{xx} =h_tg+\tfrac12hg_{xx}. \end{aligned} $$ Comparison with $f_t=h_tg+hg_t$ yields $g_t=g_{xx}/2$. Thus one backward heat factor and one forward heat factor determine the law against which the moment polynomial is integrated. For $s=-\partial_x\log g$, the source proves joint shape restrictions: on $x>0$, $r_x>0$ and $s_x\geq1/t$, both $r$ and $s$ are concave, and $H:=w/(2r)+v\leq0$ is nondecreasing. They also give $$ j:=s_x-(s/r)v=r\,\partial_x(s/r)\geq0. $$ The last inequality couples the backward gradient to the forward density; separate monotonicity and concavity do not supply it. On the first step, $s=x/t$, so concavity of $r$ gives $j\geq0$. A parabolic comparison propagates the sign within each step. At a forward jump with $k=c_+/c_-\geq1$, continuity of $\Phi$ and $f$ gives $$ r_+=kr_-,\qquad s_+=s_-+(k-1)r_-,\qquad j_+=(s_x)_+-\frac{s_+}{r_+}(r_x)_+=j_-. $$ The joint sign therefore survives coefficient jumps as well. The quotients $w/r$ and $s/r$ extend smoothly through zero because $r,s,w$ are odd and $r_x(0)>0$. The comparison's boundary controls and these extensions are analytic inputs from [OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 3.2–3.4][FS], reconstructed in [long §4.3](../long/reasoning-record.md#shape-comparisons). The factorisation of the density gives $f_x/f=r-s$. For a suitable expression $F$ in the shape quantities, define $$ \mathcal W(F)=r\partial_xF+(v+r^2-rs)F. $$ Then $f\mathcal W(F)=\partial_x(rfF)$. The smooth extensions avoid an interior boundary term at zero, and the source's differentiated Gaussian tail estimates give $rfF\to0$ at both spatial infinities for the polynomial correction used below. Hence $\mathbb E_f\mathcal W(F)=0$, where $\mathbb E_f$ denotes integration against $f(x)\,dx$. The remaining step is algebra under these analytic restrictions. The correction polynomial below is chosen by first arranging a square and other nonnegative terms containing the highest derivative $z$, then cancelling their linear terms in $z$ through the weighted divergence. The residual depends only on lower derivatives and the shape quantities. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 4.1][FS] supplies an explicit polynomial $F_2$ and a decomposition $$ z^2-12vw^2+6v^4 =\mathcal W(F_2)+\kappa v^4+\mathcal R, \qquad \mathcal R\geq0,\qquad \kappa=\frac{1661507}{1521000000}>\frac1{1000}. $$ The coefficients of $F_2$ have both signs; no sign of $F_2$ or $\mathcal W(F_2)$ is needed, since the correction integrates to zero. In contrast, the shape inequalities make every term of $\mathcal R$ nonnegative. Two of its actual terms are $$ \frac{337}{10000}\,r^2j\,(-w/r-7v)^2, \qquad (2rH_x)v\left(\frac{2331}{10000}r^2+\frac{87}{2500}j\right). $$ The first needs the joint comparison $j\geq0$; the second also uses $H_x\geq0$ on the positive half-line. Reflection preserves these signs on the negative half-line. The remaining terms use $H\leq0$, forward concavity and the other shape bounds. Thus the decomposition is positive on the shapes supplied by the PDE, not on arbitrary spatial derivatives. Integration removes $\mathcal W(F_2)$ and keeps the fourth-moment margin, giving $$ \int_{\mathbb R}(z^2-12vw^2+6v^4)f\,dx \geq\frac1{1000}\int_{\mathbb R}v^4f\,dx. \tag{5} $$ We use (5) as an imported analytic estimate. The full polynomial and its decomposition are in [Lemma 4.1 and Table 1][certificate]; Proposition 4.2 integrates them using the signs and zero boundary flux supplied by Lemma 3.4. [Long §4.4, “How the signs make a correction with zero expectation useful”](../long/reasoning-record.md#curvature-algebra) reproduces the definitions and complete identity. To obtain Lemma 2 for an integrable coefficient, choose positive monotone step coefficients $\gamma_n$ retaining the plateau near a fixed interior time, with $\|\gamma_n-\gamma\|_1\to0$, and terminal parameters $M_n\geq\|\gamma_n\|_\infty$ with $M_n\to\infty$. Spatial derivatives through order four converge uniformly on a fixed strip below one, and the diffusions driven by the same Brownian motion converge (see [OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.2 and Proposition 5.1][FS]). Only $v,w,z$ remain in (5), so no convergence theorem for the auxiliary logarithmic derivative $s$ is needed. Dividing by $c^2$ gives (3); strictness follows from $\Phi_{xx}>0$ on the plateau (see [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.3][FS]). The plateau-preserving approximants and their common strip bounds are specified in [long §4.5](../long/reasoning-record.md#plateau-limit). The zero plateau has the separate heat identity in Lemma 2. Its strictness uses a positive diffusion density and the fact that $\Phi_{xxx}$ cannot vanish identically: an even quadratic profile would contradict the one-Lipschitz bound and $|x|+O(1)$ growth. **Passage to a fixed time.** Now let $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ be continuous at $t\in(0,1)$, with $c=\gamma(t)>0$. For $0<\delta<\min(t,1-t)$ define $$ \gamma_\delta(s)= \begin{cases} c,&t-\delta\leq s0$, then $q'$ cannot attain an interior maximum. The endpoint slope bounds therefore give $q'<1$ inside the gap and the same strict area deficit. Proposition 3 supplies more for the next argument: it applies at the chosen comparison time without assuming $q''=0$, and its fourth-moment lower bound survives the local replacement. Bare strict positivity could be lost in that limit.

### 7.3 Where the strict-curvature input comes from

The proof in Section 5 used strict curvature on a positive constant
interval. We now explain how a correction with expectation zero makes
the estimate usable once the required density bounds and algebraic
identity are supplied. The sources construct the correction and prove
those bounds. Take any admissible
coefficient with $\gamma=c>0$ on an open interval, without assuming
minimality. Set $b=\Phi_{xxx}$ and $d=\Phi_{xxxx}$ there.
Differentiating the PDE and applying Itô's rule gives

$$
q''=\mathbb E[b^2-2ca^3],\qquad
q'''=\mathbb E[d^2-12cab^2+6c^2a^4].
$$

The negative middle term prevents a pointwise positivity argument.
The source instead averages with the spatial probability density
$f_t(x)$ of $X_t$ at positive time. As in the half-time example,
for any integrable function $F$, grouping paths by their reached position gives

$$
\mathbb E[F(X_t)]=\int_{\mathbb R}F(x)f_t(x)\,dx.
$$

These are probability weights on states $x$, distinct from the
Stieltjes weights $\mu_\gamma(ds)$ on overlap scales. The proof needs
bounds relating this density to the spatial derivatives of the value.
The factorisation and comparison arguments establishing those bounds
are given in [OpenAI (2026a), §3][support-signs].

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

The operation can be written directly for the positive density $f_t$;
here $f_t'$ means differentiation in the state variable $x$, with $t$ fixed.
For a smooth function $F$ with integrable terms and vanishing boundary
product $Ff_t$,

$$
\mathbb E\!\left[F'(X_t)+F(X_t)\frac{f_t'(X_t)}{f_t(X_t)}\right]
=\int_{\mathbb R}(Ff_t)'(x)\,dx=0.
$$

The source first uses positive nondecreasing finite-step coefficients with terminal approximation $M^{-1}\log(2\cosh(Mx))$, choosing $M$ at least as large as every step height. The source's sign comparisons use this bound as well as smoothness. At this stage, write $R_c=d^2-12cab^2+6c^2a^4$. The source constructs a correction $C$ from the spatial derivatives and density, with $$ \mathbb E[C(t,X_t)]=0,\qquad R_c(t,x)+C(t,x)\ge\frac{c^2}{1000}a(t,x)^4. $$ A rational polynomial identity gives the second inequality by writing the remainder as a sum of nonnegative terms. The density bounds and vanishing boundary products justify the first. Consequently $$ q'''(t)=\mathbb E[R_c(t,X_t)] =\mathbb E[(R_c+C)(t,X_t)] \ge\frac{c^2}{1000}\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]. $$ This is how the correction produces a useful lower bound for the expectation even though $R_c$ can be negative at particular states. To reach an arbitrary admissible coefficient, fix a time inside the plateau and approximate in $L^1$ by step coefficients, keeping the same value $c$ near that time. Uniform convergence of spatial derivatives through order four on a fixed strip below one, together with convergence of the coupled paths, passes the quantitative inequality to the limit. Strictness is then established for the limit itself: the constant-coefficient heat formula expresses $a$ as a nonnegative mean plus $c$ times a strictly positive variance of a nonconstant slope under a positively weighted Gaussian law. Hence $a(t,x)>0$ and its fourth moment is positive. Positivity of the approximants alone would not suffice. The auxiliary logarithmic derivatives need not converge: they have already been removed by integration. The analytic details are [OpenAI (2026a), §§3–5][support-manuscript] and the companion *Long Reasoning Record*, [§4.4, “How the signs make a correction with zero expectation useful”](../long/reasoning-record.md#curvature-algebra), and [§4.5, “A fixed-time inequality and its plateau application”](../long/reasoning-record.md#plateau-limit).
